intro: A pilot ends with a decision, and decisions are made on evidence. FDEs who can show credibly that their work moved a business metric get renewals, expansions and references; those who show a demo and anecdotes get polite thanks. This lesson covers designing the comparison so the result is believable, the confounders that fool everyone, combining adoption, quality and business metrics, turning time saved into money with honest ranges, and writing the outcome report and case study the customer's leadership will actually read.
objectives: Choose a comparison design: before and after, control group, or staggered rollout
Recognise confounders such as seasonality, selection and novelty effects
Combine adoption, quality and business metrics into one honest picture
Build an ROI estimate with explicit assumptions and ranges
Write an outcome report that leads to a clear decision

rows: Same users, metric before vs during pilot
Anything else that changed gets credited to you
Pilot users vs similar non-pilot users, same period
Groups may differ; needs enough users
Teams start at different weeks; compare each team before and after
Strong evidence with no permanent control group
Randomly route some cases to the tool
Not always acceptable to users or the business

blocks.text: Choose the design during scoping, not after the pilot, because control groups and baselines cannot be created retroactively. Where possible, use a control group or staggered rollout: they protect you against the most common objection, "maybe it was just a quiet month".

items: **Seasonality and volume**: claims spike after storms, support tickets after releases; compare like periods or use a control group.
**Selection**: if enthusiastic volunteers form the pilot group, they may have been faster anyway; compare against their own baseline or choose pilot users randomly.
**Novelty and attention**: people often perform better simply because they are being watched or have something new; look at whether gains persist after the first weeks.
**Mix shift**: if the pilot handled easier cases, average times fall for that reason alone; compare within case types.
**Process changes**: a new policy, staffing change or system upgrade during the pilot; record them in a timeline.

blocks.text: Keep a simple event log during the pilot (holidays, staffing changes, outages, releases). When a number moves, you can explain it, and you can pre-empt the sceptic in the room.

No single number convinces everyone. Present adoption (are people using it?), quality (is it right?) and business impact (did the outcome move?) together; each answers a different stakeholder's question, and a strong result on one with weakness on another is itself a finding.

Adoption tells you whether the result can scale: a big effect among three enthusiastic users is not the same as a modest effect across a whole team. Quality tells you whether speed came at the cost of correctness, the first thing a risk or compliance stakeholder will ask. Business impact is what the sponsor bought. If adoption is low, find out why before claiming success; if quality dipped, say so and show the fix.

blocks.caption: Median handling time, pilot vs control, with a bootstrap interval
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("handling_times.csv")          # columns: group, minutes
pilot = df.loc[df.group == "pilot", "minutes"].to_numpy()
control = df.loc[df.group == "control", "minutes"].to_numpy()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
diffs = [np.median(rng.choice(pilot, pilot.size)) - np.median(rng.choice(control, control.size))
         for _ in range(5000)]
low, high = np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"median pilot {np.median(pilot):.1f} min vs control {np.median(control):.1f} min")
print(f"difference 95% interval: {low:.1f} to {high:.1f} minutes")

blocks.text: Report the interval, not just the point estimate: "pilot handlers were 5 to 8 minutes faster per claim" is more honest and more persuasive than "7 minutes faster", and it tells the sponsor how sure you are. Median is usually better than mean for times, because a few very long cases distort averages.
Leaders decide on value. Translate the measured effect into money with every assumption written down and agreed with finance, and show a range rather than one optimistic figure.

blocks.caption: An ROI estimate with explicit assumptions (illustrative numbers)
blocks.code:
Measured effect:   6 min saved per claim (interval 5-8)
Volume:            9,000 claims/month in scope           (from claims system)
Loaded cost:       $45 per handler hour                  (agreed with finance)

Value per month    = 6 x 9,000 / 60 x $45 = $40,500
Value per year     = $486,000   (range: $405,000 - $648,000)
Running cost/year  = $48,000    (licences, infrastructure, model usage)
One-off cost       = $60,000    (integration and rollout)
First-year net     = $378,000   (range: $297,000 - $540,000)

items: Time saved is not money saved unless it is redeployed: say what the time enables (more claims per handler, faster customer response, less overtime).
Include quality effects where measurable: fewer errors, fewer escalations, less rework.
Include all costs honestly; a sponsor who finds a hidden cost stops trusting the whole case.
**Decision requested** at the top: expand to all motor claims teams from next quarter.
**Headline result** in one sentence with the interval.
**How it was measured**: design, period, users, confounders handled.
**Adoption, quality, impact** with one chart each.
**What did not work** and what you learned.
**Plan and costs** for the next phase, with risks.

blocks.text: With the customer's permission, turn the report into a short **case study** for your company: problem, approach, result, quote. It is one of the most valuable things an FDE produces for the business, and it becomes portfolio evidence for you.

practice.title: Analyse a pilot like a sceptic would
steps: Create a synthetic dataset of handling times for a pilot group and a control group over eight weeks, including a seasonal spike and a novelty effect that fades.
Compute a naive before/after result for the pilot group alone, then the pilot-versus-control result; explain the difference.
Compute a bootstrap interval for the median difference with the code above.
Build an ROI estimate with written assumptions and a low, central and high case.
Write a one-page outcome report following the seven steps, including a section on what did not work.
Ask a colleague to argue against your conclusion for ten minutes and add answers to their objections.

focus: Choose the comparison design during scoping, not after.
Control groups or staggered rollouts beat simple before/after.
Watch for seasonality, selection, novelty, mix shift and process changes.
Show adoption, quality and impact together.
Report intervals and ranges, with explicit, agreed assumptions.
Lead the report with the decision requested.

items.desc: Each team is its own comparison

items.syntax: value = effect x volume x unit cost

pitfalls: Deciding how to measure after the pilot, with no baseline or control.
Crediting the tool for a seasonal dip in volume.
Pilot groups of enthusiastic volunteers compared with everyone else.
One optimistic ROI figure with hidden assumptions.
Reports that bury the decision on page four.

quiz.q: Handling time fell 20% during a pilot that ran in a quiet month. Which design best rules out seasonality?
options: A control group of similar users measured over the same period
A longer before-and-after window for pilot users
Asking pilot users if they felt faster
Excluding the slowest week from the data
quiz.explain: A control group experiences the same season and volume, so the difference between groups isolates the effect of the tool.

quiz.q: Why report a median with a bootstrap interval for handling times?
options: Medians resist long-tail cases and the interval shows uncertainty
Means are not allowed for time measurements
Bootstrap intervals always make results look larger
Medians require fewer data points to compute
quiz.explain: A few very long cases distort means; the interval tells the sponsor how confident to be in the effect size.

quiz.q: Pilot users were volunteers who asked to join. What risk does that create?
options: Selection bias: they may have been faster or keener anyway
Seasonality, because volunteers join in summer
Mix shift in the types of claims processed
None, because volunteers are representative
quiz.explain: Self-selected groups differ from the population; compare them with their own baseline or choose pilot users randomly.

quiz.q: Which ROI presentation is most credible to a finance team?
options: Low, central and high cases with assumptions they agreed
One headline figure based on the best week
Savings without mentioning running costs
A projection to all departments in the company
quiz.explain: Explicit, agreed assumptions and ranges survive scrutiny; optimistic single numbers and hidden costs do not.

quiz.q: What should appear first in an outcome report?
options: The decision you are asking the sponsor to make
A detailed history of the technical architecture
Thanks to everyone involved in the pilot
The full raw dataset
quiz.explain: Leaders read the top first; leading with the decision and headline result focuses everything that follows.
